📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’ve decided to host a gathering and spent far more time and money on it than you expected.
  • It has been revealed that or maybe everything has lined up perfectly for your event and then one of your guests arrives and tells you that they forgot to mention that they don’t eat gluten, dairy, meat, beans, fiber, or sugar and now you feel totally unprepared.
  • Suddenly your perfect event is going sideways and you find yourself looking for a crawlspace to hide in or someone to snap at.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Does this sound familiar? You’ve decided to host a gathering and spent far more time and money on it than you expected. But that’s OK. Because you really wanted to extend yourself, but now you are just a little more frazzled than you wanted to be. But you ignore your difficult feelings and press on.

It has been revealed that or maybe everything has lined up perfectly for your event and then one of your guests arrives and tells you that they forgot to mention that they don’t eat gluten, dairy, meat, beans, fiber, or sugar and now you feel totally unprepared. Or maybe a well-meaning family member says something they think is funny, and you find it hurtful and it makes you want to close down.

Suddenly your perfect event is going sideways and you find yourself looking for a crawlspace to hide in or someone to snap at. These are the moments when mindfulness can help us pause, take a breath, and acknowledge that things aren’t going as planned. Rather than getting swept up in frustration, we can reconnect with our original intention: bringing people together in a welcoming, loving atmosphere.

According to recent reports, social gatherings can give us a rich and wonderful opportunity to strengthen bonds of love and connection. But even the best-laid plans can rapidly turn into emotional meltdowns unless we make a point of pausing to recognize when we get caught up in the impossible task of trying to get everything right.

Sources indicate that instead, you can strategy a upcoming kind of to-do list. One that puts self-care and the creation of a loving atmosphere as the top priority.

Sources indicate that I am usually the person in my family who hosts the celebrations. Yet every year, I seem to get amnesia about how tired, overwhelmed, and irritated I feel by the time the first person gets there.

According to recent reports, I go the extra mile to make an overflowing amount of  hand crafted food. I take time to create a charming atmosphere. But by the time my guests arrive, I have barely slept in a week and have long forgotten why I wanted to bring everyone together in the first place. Somewhere along the way, my self-imposed expectations had taken over. Instead of being the warm, welcoming host I’d hoped to be, I became the anxious, overburdened kitchen help, desperately trying to keep the food train going.

It has been revealed that during a particularly big event when I really tried to outdo myself, a close friend and two family members told me I seemed uptight and terse. And, as if that weren’t enough, they didn’t like my tone!

It has been revealed that “You don’t like my TONE? What? How dare you! Ungrateful clods.”.

After skulking away in a state of icy fury, my years of mindfulness practice eventually kicked in and a few hundred breaths later I managed to notice how I had lost sight of my heartfelt intention of creating a welcoming haven for love and connection.

Instead, I’d become so focused on getting everything done that I’d turned the gathering into a military operation.

I regularly remind myself how valuable it is when I take a moment to be curious, rather than certain. When I could finally get there, my investigations helped me notice that my shoulders were up and I was holding my breath.

I could feel the tightness in my face every time someone interrupted me with their warm hellos. I could recognize that somewhere along the way, I had lost sight of my true desire to help nourish joy for myself and everyone else.

Expecting ourselves to regulate our emotions perfectly in the middle of a difficult moment is asking a lot.

I needed some space and time to process what had happened before I could do anything other than snap at someone or run away.

Although I was too reactive in the moment to appreciate the honest feedback about my tone, once I had time to step back and reflect, I could recognize and accept, without having to like it, that  my tone was sharp, and not in keeping with my intention for the event.

At the same time, looking more closely at my reactions helped me see how worn out I was feeling and that I really needed to offer myself wisdom and self-care.

So what can mindfulness offer us in moments like these?

Mindfulness is an umbrella that contains practices to help calm our nervous system, stabilize the mind and emotions, be more in touch with our bodies and give us ways to practice anchoring our attention in the present.

This may sound boringly obvious, but if you pay attention, you might notice how often your mind swings between thoughts of the past and fears about the future, spending surprisingly little time in the present.

In a recent development, mindfulness is the encouragement to recognize that the attitude you bring to your moment-by-moment experiences has a great effect on your body’s stress response. You can notice whether being patient leads to greater feelings of peace more than being impatient. Mindfulness attitudes include acceptance, gratitude, and generosity. What do you notice about how it makes you feel to practice these attitudes?

According to recent reports, mindfulness can help you see the importance of non-judgement to help you have a wider view, and to cultivate the possibility of seeing and experiencing the world with fewer biases. Just like any learned skill, it is a practice and is strengthened through repetition.

In my case, it took me a while to see that I was doing things the same way every year, hoping for a different result. Only after several people irritated me with their honesty did I let myself notice whether I might be more uptight than I realized. By recognizing my reactions without judging myself, I could see how I might want to do things differently in the future so I could enjoy the gathering alongside my guests.

But first I had to notice what I was doing in the present, and check in regularly to confirm that I was following through on my intention to put connection above trying to turn my place into a pop-up restaurant.

Industry observers note that it takes practice to be super irritated and still be able to step back and be curious about what has grabbed you. Making time to include practical mindful moments, every day, like noticing impatience, or choosing friendliness, can be so helpful as a way to cultivate enough mindful muscle to support you  when the substantial life moments can feel so clobbering.

If someone doesn’t like your tone, or you don’t like theirs, how can you meet that moment without it demolishing you or them?

Originally developed by Michele McDonald and later adapted and popularized by Tara Brach, the R.A.I.N practice offers one way to respond:.

Notice what’s happening at the moment. Maybe you’re feeling irritated, hurt, overwhelmed, or defensive. You don’t have to respond immediately or change how you feel. Simply begin by recognizing what’s present.

Allow yourself to acknowledge the experience, even if it’s uncomfortable. You don’t have to like what’s happening or agree with someone else’s behavior. Acceptance simply means recognizing what you’re feeling without fighting against it.

Bring some curiosity to your reaction. What might have triggered it? What thoughts are running through your mind? Where do you notice tension or discomfort in your body? You might recognize feelings of anger, disappointment, or exhaustion beneath your initial reaction. See whether you can explore what’s happening without judging yourself for it.

Offer yourself a little care and compassion. Maybe that means placing a hand over your heart, stepping away for a few quiet moments, resting, or getting something to eat. Consider what might help you feel supported rather than adding more pressure to an already difficult moment.

Gatherings and celebrations offer opportunities for generosity, joy, and connection, especially when we remember why we wanted to come together in the first place.

Even the happiest occasions can bring moments of stress or frustration.

Practicing R.A.I.N can help us reconnect with our intentions and meet difficult moments with kindness and compassion. And when things don’t go quite as planned, keeping a teensy sense of humor doesn’t hurt, either.

It has been revealed that elaine Smookler, RP, is a Registered Psychotherapist, mindfulness teacher, speaker, writer, and performer. A founding faculty member of the Centre for Mindfulness Studies in Toronto, she has taught Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) and Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR), and has delivered mindfulness training through the University of Toronto Faculty of Medicine, SickKids Hospital, and the University of Toronto School of Continuing Studies.

Elaine created and taught “A Mindful Way Through the Creative Process” and contributed to the certificate program “Mindfulness-Informed End-of-Life Care.” Her work has brought mindfulness training to a remarkably diverse range of audiences, including healthcare professionals, educators, parole officers, employee assistance programs, corporate teams, entrepreneurs, children, and teens.

As a psychotherapist, Elaine helps clients navigate life’s challenges with practical, evidence-informed tools grounded in mindfulness, self-compassion, and emotional resilience. She is also a guide for the Dawn Personalized Cancer Stewardship Program, supporting individuals facing cancer and complex health journeys.

Beyond her clinical and teaching work, Elaine explores mindfulness, creativity, and the human experience as a keynote speaker, columnist, stand-up comedian, actor, and singer, bringing warmth, insight, and humour to every stage and conversation.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information.
  • Sources indicate that the conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown.
  • Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

Sources indicate that the conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech company on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

Fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the issue, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Sources indicate that without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

Recent findings suggest that given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so new. Striking the balance was critical.

The result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

Recent findings suggest that the WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

According to recent reports, WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

According to recent reports, an crucial first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

Inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

It has been revealed that our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

To further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

Recent findings suggest that the brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

It has been revealed that WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

It has been revealed that buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

In a recent development, BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term plans, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

The "interest-free" label on short-term prepares deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies reveals that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

According to recent reports, the financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

Recent findings suggest that A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL users have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound rapidly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

Industry observers note that the credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing plans to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

For anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

It has been revealed that there is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a latest dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

The financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something important.

It has been revealed that the question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

In a recent development, for those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most notable variable in determining how swiftly you reach FI.

Industry observers note that mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL aims — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening newly introduced ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded firm (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

Sources indicate that increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing plans report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

Industry observers note that afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

In a recent development, klarna's "Pay in 4" proposal is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing prepares charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

Industry observers note that it is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently demonstrates that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most users, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

It has been revealed that because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

In a recent development, buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL people spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.

It has been revealed that cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks. Chef Chuy Villarreal cooks regional cuisine as an evolution of the Regiomontana barbecue, and Anagrama answers with a system borrowed from the hand-painted business signs of downtown Monterrey. Black fields carry the shouting, orange paper carries the warmth, and a smiling face and a small cow sit beside the wordmark like a stamp.

Industry observers note that the logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point. Anagrama drew a custom typeface, Lechon Sans, from the same source, built for social media lockups that spotlight a single word. The specimen highlights the full set: capitals, numerals, punctuation, arrows, and small symbols that include the smiley face, the cow, and a pig.

Industry observers note that the lockups take their cues from Mercado Juarez, the downtown market where the studio photographed signs to dress the restaurant walls. Phrases stack in mixed sizes with quotation marks doing the work of a frame: BARBACOA, LECHON, CABRITO. VINOS NATURALES, BIEN FRIOS. GRAN DOMINGO. A word goes huge when it matters, small when it is a wink, and the quotes and rules hold the pieces together.

According to recent reports, the posters are physical objects first. One orange sheet curls at the corner against a black field, its type running diagonally across the page. A kraft sheet carries the same treatment, the paper grain showing through the ink. The black behind both does quiet work: it makes the orange and the kraft read as light in a dark room.

The system spreads across everything a guest can hold. Tote bags run in cream, green, and orange, each carrying a different phrase, and a yellow cattle ear tag hangs from the handles as the label. Business cards take the same marks in gold foil, the cow and the smiley pressed small into white stock.

Inside the restaurant the identity turns architectural. A neon CARA DE VACA sign glows red over the entrance at night: the logo lettering, now in light. Wood and metal frame the room, brand marks sit on walls and mirrors, and plants soften the space around the central bar, where natural wines and Mexican distillates pour.

The website carries the same voice, quieter: the personality, the menu photos, a reservation button, and the address. Social posts use the lockups the typeface was built for, phrases set large enough to read at a scroll. From a neon sign to a phone screen, the identity never changes its register.

‘I want the experiences I had to be available forever’: arts figures and scientists hit out at proposed job cuts at Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution.
  • It has been revealed that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.

It has been revealed that TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).

Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.

It has been revealed that staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.

However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.

This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”.

“I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and Newly introduced Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.

In a recent development, the proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a plan to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.

According to recent reports, although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a new organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry states. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.

Asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he says.

TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.

According to recent reports, according to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a upcoming government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, indicates Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.

According to recent reports, A state government spokesperson states there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a fresh A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”.

In a recent development, the proposed cuts to staff numbers are presently under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both problems are expected on Tuesday 24 November.

At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have mentioned they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.
  • Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.
  • Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

Sources indicate that “This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”.

“The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them,” he continued.

“That fusion is at the heart of this project – how do these technologies, through cultural practices on the ground, begin to morph into new creatures and new constellations that people try to make sense of to interpret the violence of this military technology that is taking place.”.

Nahleh and Saloojee aimed to combine the reality of modern war with mythical storytelling, drawing upon their research into communities exposed to military attacks.

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing newly introduced mythical creatures – creatures that fuse together technological advancement with epistemic practices and myth-making practices that happen from the ground,” said Nahleh.

“Most of these creatures, these modern constellations as we’re calling them, are populating the night sky in our drawing alongside pathways of flights of drones, satellites and other things that manifest across the night sky we’ve inherited, rather than the one we lost,” he continued.

“We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us, be it in the shape of missiles, phosphorus, or flares.”.

As well as depicting creature-like constellations in their inner curves, the structures themselves were designed as creatures – the nocturnal Solifugi spider known to run out the sun and into shade.

According to recent reports, “The project is dedicated to the Solifugi, which is a spider that by nature runs away from the sun, the sun of imperial savagery,” remarked Nahleh. “It has a very thick skin to protect it from this brightness, and in its belly is a map of the contemporary sky.”.

Sources indicate that three openings puncture the shell in each of the installations. In the desert site at Al Madam, a vertical cut-out frames a view of the minaret of a distant mosque, and at the slaughterhouse site, a long opening was set at the height of a cow.

Traditional Hakawati storytellers will narrate stories at the installations as part of the triennial, which runs until April.

Recent findings suggest that “The story is difficult, but it’s about finding optimism,” said Nahleh. “People are carving their own histories on the weapons that are here to annihilate them.”.

It has been revealed that “There’s a paradox here that we have to confront,” he continued. “When libraries are being erased, and people have no more books to publish or things to write on, they’re writing on the weapons that are sent to devour them.”.

“Kids now are finding ways again to dream by placing their wishes upon the shooting stars, which are usually missiles and rockets. It’s a sad and complicated story, but we can no longer escape it by wishing for a sky we no longer have.”.

We rounded up eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which includes a draping shelter that pays homage to the improvised learning spaces created by Virginia’s Black community, and a circular canopy with cut-outs that plot 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun.

Friday Five With Sarah Meyohas: Art, Science, and AI in ‘Phase Transition’

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In 2015, Meyohas released Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

In 2015, Meyohas released Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

It has been revealed that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the Latest Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

For today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her fresh installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

“The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

The work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she says. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

That initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

What began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas notes. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

It has been revealed that that ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas states. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

According to recent reports, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

In a recent development, neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

According to recent reports, photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Recent findings suggest that “Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Industry observers note that teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

According to recent reports, “I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

Phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

Founder Alex Crowder sought to move beyond the conventions of traditional floristry websites, creating instead a platform that could house her studio’s portfolio while articulating their deeper philosophy of working with nature rather than against it.

Drawing from historical horticultural publications, plant glossaries and garden almanacs, 1/1 Studio developed a design language that honours the depth of knowledge and integrity inherent in Field Studies Flora’s practice. The site functions as both a gallery of case studies and an educational resource, inviting visitors into a world where botanical understanding and artistic expression converge.

The visual identity and website design emphasise documentation and craft, mirroring the studio’s meticulous approach to their work. A film by Scott Macdonough, shot in the fields of Massachusetts, unveils the homepage, setting the tone for work born from connection to the natural world.

The printed materials extend this language, creating a cohesive system that supports Field Studies Flora’s position at the intersection of horticulture, design and environmental stewardship. Typography and layout choices reference archival botanical texts, lending the contemporary practice a sense of scholarly rigor.

#217859. Industry News: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Design-milk ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we rolled out The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we rolled out The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out blueprint. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

Sources indicate that we spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

One of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

Sources indicate that in my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

In a recent development, confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

I’m a significant believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

Clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to plan? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

Recent findings suggest that this sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

Kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

My mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

According to recent reports, my conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

We talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

Recent findings suggest that in my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

In a recent development, we’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

It has been revealed that if you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, new perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

Industry observers note that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Sources indicate that caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Major Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a fresh group exhibition.

Geometric metalwork, organic silhouettes, and carved wood offer contrasting interpretations of the traditional candelabra. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

Sources indicate that titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Industry observers note that the results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

Recent findings suggest that from a sculptural glass candelabra to a beaded floor-standing candleholder, the exhibition explores the relationship between materiality, scale, and function. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Firm, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

Recent findings suggest that industrial forms mingle with playful figurative designs, including a carved wooden dog and a sculptural arrangement of flowers. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Industry observers note that timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

Candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, Upcoming York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

In a recent development, lit candles cast warm pools of light and shadows across the surrounding surfaces, bringing another dimension to the sculptural objects. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack.
  • Of course, presentation matters, too.
  • Industry observers note that italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Industry observers note that italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Industry observers note that from Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

Sources indicate that from cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Sources indicate that porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

It has been revealed that long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Industry News: Art Meets the Slopes at Powder Mountain’s Outdoor Gallery

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings.
  • Recent findings suggest that davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain.
  • Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings. After all, ski resorts typically offer great mountain views. But at Powder Mountain in Utah, visitors get more than a scenic view. They might also encounter a bright pink pineapple rising among the pines, a classical Greek column twisted into an improbable shape, or poetry carved into a boulder. These three installations are the latest additions to Powder Art Foundation’s skiable outdoor art museum, an evolving collection that challenges how—and where—we experience art.

Recent findings suggest that davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography courtesy of Powder Art Foundation.

Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains. The foundation’s goal is to bring contemporary installations into dialogue with the landscape while honoring the region’s connection to the Land Art movement.

“We’re building a collection that people encounter while spending time outdoors, so I’m interested in work that can surprise you and hold your attention without needing a museum around it,” indicates Alex Zhang, chief creative officer of Powder Mountain.

Schemata Architects Designs a Modern Chalet on Powder Mountain.

Sources indicate that this year’s new installations—from artists Jenny Holzer, Rose Wylie, and Xu Zhen—join an existing collection that includes works by Davina Semo, Nobuo Sekine, Nancy Holt, Kayode Ojo, and others. Each takes a different approach to interacting with the landscape. “I like having that range, rather than one consistent approach to what outdoor sculpture should look like,” Zhang says.

Jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026), featuring poetry by May Swenson carved into a native quartzite boulder, sits within the forested landscape of Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Whether skiing in winter or hiking and biking during warmer months, visitors may encounter THE EYE (2026), a newly introduced installation by Jenny Holzer. The American neo-conceptual artist conceived of an evolving commission for Powder Mountain centered on work by the late Utah-born poet May Swenson.

Holzer selected a native quartzite boulder already embedded in the mountain, carving a phrase from Swenson’s poetry directly into the stone rather than relocating it or disturbing the surrounding vegetation: “The eye also a sun wanders and all that it sees it owns.”.

A close-up of Jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026) reveals a line of poetry by May Swenson carved directly into a native quartzite boulder at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Sources indicate that blending into its natural surroundings, the work could easily go unnoticed by visitors who aren’t looking carefully. As snow, sunlight, and vegetation transform the landscape throughout the year, the inscription offers a point of continuity, even as the experience of encountering it changes.

THE EYE is the first in what Holzer plans to be an ongoing group of carved stones across the mountain. Like this one, future boulders will be selected on the mountain and the art created in place.

Sources indicate that rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025), a 12-foot-tall painted bronze sculpture inspired by a pineapple she sketched in 2013, stands among towering pine trees at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

A decidedly different approach comes from Rose Wylie, whose Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb (2025) takes the form of a 12-foot-tall, bright pink painted bronze sculpture. The pineapple-like totem marks Wylie’s first permanent public sculpture in the U.S. The 92-year-old British painter describes the work as “poetic transformation,” which began in 2013 when she purchased a Ghanaian-grown pineapple at a local market. Struck by its distinctive surface and dramatic crown of leaves, she sketched the fruit.

A close-up of Rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025) highlights the exaggerated crown of leaves that gives the bright pink sculpture its distinctive silhouette. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

It has been revealed that more than a decade later, those drawings have taken on a latest dimension. Standing among 50-foot pine trees, the painted bronze sculpture retains the exaggerated silhouette of Wylie’s original sketches. Its form shifts between recognizable fruit, fantastical plant, and something more explosive, suggesting how scale and material can transform an ordinary subject into something entirely unexpected.

Industry observers note that unlike Holzer’s work, which is quite literally part of the scenery, Wylie’s is impossible to miss, its almost cartoonish silhouette creating an unexpected interruption in the natural landscape. Shanghai-based artist Xu Zhen takes yet another approach with Hello (2021–2022), which transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine form.

Xu Zhen’s ‘Hello’ (2021–2022) transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine sculpture nestled among the aspen trees at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

It has been revealed that to develop the sculpture’s serpentine form, Zhen studied the movements of snakes alongside representations of dragons and serpents from different cultures. He ultimately selected the Corinthian column for its ornate capital, whose leaf-like details suggested the head of a living creature. Using a 3D-scanned model as his starting point, he developed the form digitally before producing a full-scale prototype that informed the final bronze casting.

“My work has always been about discovering alternative forms that an object might take,” the multimedia artist explains. “These forms should feel natural, as though the object was always meant to exist that way, while remaining outside our conventional understanding and experience.”.

Sources indicate that A close-up of Xu Zhen’s Hello (2021–2022) reveals the ornate Corinthian capital, whose leaf-like details give the twisting column an almost creature-like appearance. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that installed among the mountain’s aspen trees, Hello takes on what Zhen describes as a “distinctly surreal quality.” Yet the setting also feels surprisingly natural. When he first saw the sculpture at Powder Mountain, the artist recalls feeling “that it had returned to the world where it belongs.”.

It has been revealed that for Zhang, the experience of encountering these works is as important as the artworks themselves. “You’re moving, your heart rate is up, there’s adrenaline, and then you come around a corner and encounter a work without expecting it,” he says. “I think being that engaged in your body changes how you experience the art.”.

Visitors to Powder Art Foundation’s fall open house gather around Nobuo Sekine’s Phase of Nothingness – Stone Stack (1970/2025) at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by McCade Gordon for Powder Art Foundation.

According to recent reports, not every work is intended to have the same relationship to the mountain. “Some should feel like you discovered them; others should stop you in your tracks,” Zhang claims. “The mountain connects everything.”.

It has been revealed that the Powder Mountain art trail opens for the winter season in mid-December, with lift-accessible installations available from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily and night access to the Sundown area from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Access to the installations is included with a lift ticket or season pass.

Industry observers note that dalene Rovenstine is a New York–based writer and editor covering design, architecture, and lifestyle. She enjoys trying new restaurants, cheering on the Oklahoma City Thunder, and watching far too much TV. Her writing has appeared in Entertainment Weekly, TV Guide, Popular Mechanics, Hamptons, Luxe Interiors + Design, Interior Design, and more.

💡 Key Takeaways
